title: Jensen Huang and Silicon Valley’s Short-Term Thinking
summary: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket CastsJust like that, Jensen Huang is back on top. Reportedly, President Trump called Nvidia’s board and encouraged it to reinstate the former CEO, who had been pushed out only two weeks earlier. The board made the “correct and pr...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Just like that, Jensen Huang is back on top. Reportedly, President Trump called Nvidia’s board and encouraged it to reinstate the former CEO, who had been pushed out only two weeks earlier. The board made the “correct and proper decision,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, which ensures the “Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The president seemed happy. Tech leaders were relieved. The stock market seemed to rally with the news. A lot of other interested parties, however, still have burning questions.

Lawmakers from both parties are planning to grill Huang about the affair he had with a suspected Chinese spy and the related threats to national security. But how will Americans, who just voted resoundingly against AI, data centers, and grift among the rich, receive the president giving a pass to his tech-CEO friend? On this episode of Radio Atlantic, Charlie Warzel talks about Nvidia, Huang, the short-term thinking of tech CEOs, and an economy held hostage by AI.


The following is a transcript of the episode:

Charlie Warzel: We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips. And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare. I really do.

[Music]

Hanna Rosin: Today, Jensen Huang was reinstated as chairman of Nvidia, the chip-manufacturing giant. Elon Musk posted on X, “The mistake has been corrected.” The president referred to it as the “correct and proper decision” and posted an AI-generated meme showing Huang in the same raised-fist pose that Trump himself adopted after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania.

So for the president, for Huang, and for other tech giants: order restored. For a lot of other people, though—what?

I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic.

It’s been just about two weeks since Huang, who is close to the president, admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Congressional leaders are at this very moment continuing to call up Huang to testify about the dangers his affair posed to national security.

The showdown with China over spying, over AI dominance, is still a looming threat of our era. And yet, there is Huang, right back in his corner office with his latest leather jacket.

Joining me to discuss is tech writer and host of the Galaxy Brain podcast Charlie Warzel.

Charlie, we are here once again talking about the story that never stops giving. Welcome to the show.

Warzel: Thank you for having me. I told you this is the nightmare scenario two weeks ago, and here we are in the nightmare.

Rosin: I knew that was my first question. So when you woke up this morning to the news that Huang was reinstated at Nvidia, do you think, No way? Or I knew this was gonna happen. I told you so?

Warzel: Somewhere in between, honestly. It was starting to get—on Sunday, [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent sort of walked back a little bit. He was on—I believe on CBS—one of the morning shows, and he initially took this very strident position that the Nvidia board needed to look outside the company for leadership. And then when pressed on it again, he kind of backtracked and said, Well, you know, Jensen Huang is actually now on the outside. And so that signaled a little to me that this week could get a little crazy. I didn’t anticipate it happening this quickly, though.

Rosin: I mean, there has been a lot of reporting that President Trump was involved in the decision, that he called into the Nvidia board meeting to advocate for the return of Huang. What do we know so far about the president’s involvement?

Warzel: I mean, this is—I don’t know if it’s unprecedented. But this is a lot of involvement from the president of the United States in a publicly traded company’s personnel decisions to—he said he both intervened directly and indirectly, whatever indirectly means. But there were calls, supposedly. There have been communications over the recent weeks with Trump and Jensen Huang, who are cellphone buddies. It’s remarkable.

The hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman said that the wisdom of the crowd has spoken, which I think is a very odd way to describe the president of the United States intervening in the workings of a corporate board. But hey, the wisdom of a crowd has spoken, I guess.

Rosin: Okay, so what we know so far is that the president was probably heavily involved in the decision to return back to the top of this company someone who was implicated in a national-security scandal. So it’s not obvious why a president would intervene in that way. So let’s unpack it a little bit. One theory why Trump would intervene in this way is the economy, right?

Warzel: So there’s a lot here. As we talked about on a previous episode of this, as a lot of people, including myself, have written about and reported on: Nvidia, in some ways, can be seen as , like, a load-bearing block of the global economy, right? They both power the AI boom with their chips. They also invest into the AI companies through this, like, five-layer cake that Jensen Huang helped create, the circular financing, right? So they both power the boom; they finance the boom. That makes them very critical to the global economy. There are a lot of people who argue that Jensen Huang essentially, like, is the one man whose fate determines whether the market goes up and down.

Nvidia stock for a while was down, but the rest of the economy was doing okay. It was kind of shouldering this. And then late last week, there was a pretty big sell-off led by a lot of tech stocks. And a lot of the year’s gains in the S&P 500 were lost. So people were kind of freaking out. I think it’s also no coincidence that this was announced—Huang’s reinstatement came—just, you know, right before the markets opened on Monday, after this huge sell-off on Friday. So the economy is a big part of this. Donald Trump believes, according to all the reporting that we’ve seen, that Jensen Huang is a critical part of the AI boom, which is, you know, propping up the rest of the stock market.

Rosina: So it’s not just that Nvidia is too big to fail. It too much of a risk. It’s Jensen Wang, specifically?

Warzel: That’s the belief. I mean, that’s at least what a lot of these tech leaders are saying too. So there’s really, like, three cohorts that have been agitating for this. One is Nvidia shareholders, who, obviously, Jensen Huang has made them tons and tons of money, especially if you’ve been a shareholder for a very long time in the company. But even anyone who got in after the ChatGPT revolution has seen huge gains, a stock split. So they want this guy back because he’s made them a lot of money.

Then you have the Silicon Valley–elite class. I would argue the Silicon Valley–elite class wants this because they want the AI boom to continue. They have a lot riding on this. All the AI CEOs have a whole bunch of investments of their own that are predicated on all the numbers going up and up and up.

But also, I think, there’s a cultural reason for this, which is: They do not want to see arguably the greatest visionary, the most irreplaceable CEO in Silicon Valley ousted, because it means that they could be ousted. It means that the CEO is vulnerable, that the visionary founder is vulnerable. I think that’s, like, a very big part of this. This is one of the existential crises that these guys have been going through, because everyone thought that Jensen was too big to fail. The fact that he had to resign after all this pressure and the board didn’t want him back is, I think to them, a very, very scary proposition because it means they can no longer act with impunity. So that was one of the reasons.

And then I think you have Donald Trump, who wanted the economy to keep going on his watch, and this was the thing, the lever he thought he could pull to make number go up.

Rosin: So it’s like there’s a Silicon Valley myth of a genius, and Trump has used the word genius recently. And that’s a cultural trope, but it’s also real because it drives the stock market. So it’s kind of a circular logic around this word visionary and genius that you just mentioned.

Warzel: Yeah, I mean, I think that so much of stock markets, it’s a confidence game. And I don’t mean that in the sense of: It’s a con. I mean, it’s about having confidence in the market, having confidence in the direction of things.

For so long, we have been talking about the economy as being propped up by AI, and we’ve been talking about AI in America as having all this very peculiar circular financing, about Is this a bubble? Is this not a bubble? And there’s this idea around all of it of extreme precarity, right? That all of this is contingent on a big bet that has been made, both about the technology succeeding but also about all of this different type of financing and all this historic investment actually meaning something and going somewhere.

You need confidence from all of these investors, from all of these folks. Jensen Huang is somebody who, for this class of people, projected a lot of confidence and instilled a lot of confidence in the direction of where the economy and where the AI boom is going. So with him out of it, there was a lot of uncertainty. We were starting to see that in the markets. This freaked a lot of people out.

Rosin: Right, and they don’t like uncertainty. Okay, let me run another Trump motivation by you. Lately, Trump has been talking about Alice Huang—the woman who Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with and who U.S. intelligence officials are suspecting to be a spy—has been sort of diminishing her role.

He said recently, “Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy.” Now we’ve heard this from the president, not from U.S. intelligence officials. And I was wondering if there’s something in here about Trump minimizing affairs because of his own history, sort of minimizing the importance of this kind of scandal taking down a great leader.

Warzel: I think it’s not only just Trump; it’s all these folks we’re talking about in Silicon Valley. They’ve all been approaching this scandal not from the geopolitical angle of this, but from the moral-infidelity angle, right? Saying, you know, Everyone has their foibles; everyone is flawed; geniuses can be flawed too. Everyone deserves a second chance. And it’s really not a question about morality.

There’s obviously, you know, the corporate-HR level of things, which is that there’s been reporting about Huang having affairs with employees in the company, including a direct report. Alice Huang was also a client of Nvidia’s, of Jensen Huang, so there’s an impropriety there. But that’s not the thing that people, that lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are upset about right now. They’re upset about the fact that Alice Huang has this alleged tie to Chinese intelligence, and what, if anything, this did to the larger geopolitical question: whether Megaspeed, this company she worked with, was skirting U.S. chip-export bans, allowing Nvidia chips to get into China or to be used by China in these remote-access data centers; or whether or not Alice Huang was reporting on things that Jensen Huang was doing; whether she had access to any of his devices or anything like that—all of those geopolitical concerns.

So it’s interesting to watch both Trump and all these executives sort of not talk about that, and just focus on this other morality play. But I think what we know is actually very troubling. There’s good evidence to suggest that a lot of chip-smuggling was going on. We don’t know whether Huang and Nvidia were directly related to this, but we know that Megaspeed certainly had some role to play in this ecosystem. And Megaspeed, it should be said, has declined all allegations of wrongdoing here. And The New York Times reported on Sunday that Alice Huang had been keeping in touch with an agent in the Chinese intelligence service for over a year. She’d been speaking with this person and staying in contact with them while she was maintaining this relationship with Jensen Huang. So that’s a lot of time. And it’s very interesting to see that report come out on Sunday and have him get reinstated on Monday.

[Music]

Rosin: When we come back, we talk about how this is more than just an economic story.

[Break]

Rosin: So right now, at this moment, there are two camps. There’s the President Trump–Jensen Huang tech-leader camp. They want Jensen Huang to come back. But the other track, which is the national-security track, is continuing to move forward. Congressional leaders are still asking Jensen Huang to come and testify. And polls show that Americans actually do care about the national-security risks involved here. So presumably, the story—you and I are gonna be talking about this again. This story is not going to go away.

Let’s take the congressional testimonies first. What does it look like if you have Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, testifying before Congress with the president’s backing—as opposed to what could have been, which is Jensen Huang, a citizen, not beholden to the company, not the CEO, and without the support of the president?

Warzel: In an interesting way, this is just a way bigger scandal now. Like, this is a way bigger, thornier, more intense, more interesting scandal. Which, again, if you’re Donald Trump—and, also, people who care about, you know, Nvidia’s relationship to the global economy and the AI boom—the logic doesn’t fully make sense there, right? You would probably want this to go away rather than become, like, the central story of Washington, D.C., for the next 12 months or so. It remains to be seen whether Huang will just come there and plead the Fifth, right? Just say, like, absolutely nothing because basically anything he could say seems like it may or may not jeopardize Nvidia’s position, a bunch of other people. He is now in charge of this company.

It’s also going to absolutely invigorate the investigations, again, which you’re seeing are coming from both China hawks or just people who are very upset about the way that this has been handled by the Trump administration and Trump’s involvement in getting him reinstated.

I sort of don’t have words for how charged this is going to be. We just had an election where, as you alluded to, America expressed deep concern with artificial intelligence in general, with data centers, which are the thing that house all the Nvidia chips. And you have a class of new lawmakers who are coming in with a mandate from America to try to rein in this, like, tech-elite class, this AI economy that people feel is akin to a hostage situation, right? You have all of these people saying, If you don’t let us build what we wanna do and act the way that we wanna do, then the numbers gonna go down. All this, you know—the bubble’s gonna pop, and good luck, right? Nice economy you got there; hope nothing happens to it, sort of situation. You’re gonna have, like, all of that collide in D.C., and I think it’s gonna be a nightmare. I really do.

Rosin: Yeah, that’s absolutely correct because if there is one desire from this midterm flip, it’s accountability. Like, let us enter an era of accountability where rich people don’t get to get away with whatever they want to get away with. That’s what the people seem to be asking for, both in their concerns about corruption, their concerns about data centers, everything that you just mentioned. And this just feels like a sort of pushback to all that.

Warzel: Absolutely. And I think that a lot of people are gonna have stuff to prove here, right? They’re gonna wanna make an example out of all of this. And I was talking to somebody in Silicon Valley this morning about this, and they were saying to me that the election really showed this really short-term political thinking, right? The tech leaders were so focused on the AI bet that they allowed themselves to get caught up in, you know, hitching their wagon to Trump and the MAGA situation, right? Like, all the donations for the ballroom, the standing behind him at the inauguration, all of the meetings, the fawning, and all of that. And not seeing that the political winds could blow, you know, in other directions, that hitching your star to this guy so completely was a bad calculation. It’s because they had this short-term thinking.

And this person described this to me as, like, another perfect example of the short-term thinking. Like, yes, we solved this problem in the very near term. The stock market is gonna rally now on all of this. But what’s it gonna mean for this to become a far bigger political scandal? Like, what is that going to mean potentially to, you know, how the Democrats are going to position themselves against AI in 2028? Like, it seems like they are playing checkers instead of, you know, the seven-dimensional chess that they always claim to be playing.

Rosin: Yeah. Well, Charlie, it looks like there’s gonna be a showdown, and I look forward to talking to you about it when it unfolds. Thank you so much for explaining this to us.

Warzel: Yeah. Absolutely. Happy to be here.

Rosin: That is all for today’s show.

[Music]

Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here today, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can find them on The Atlantic’s YouTube page. You can find them on Apple or Spotify or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And you can subscribe to this publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Hanna Rosin.

title: The Economy Is a Hostage Situation
summary: If there was ever any doubt, it ought to be silenced now. You, me, and Donald Trump—we all live in an Nvidia-state. What you need to know about living in an Nvidia-state is that it is not a democracy. Nor is it ruled by a benevolent king. Instead, the Nvidia-state governs via the logic of a hostage ...
content:
If there was ever any doubt, it ought to be silenced now. You, me, and Donald Trump—we all live in an Nvidia-state. What you need to know about living in an Nvidia-state is that it is not a democracy. Nor is it ruled by a benevolent king. Instead, the Nvidia-state governs via the logic of a hostage situation. You have two choices: Let AI rip while tech leaders act with impunity, or watch the economy enter a recession.

[Read: ]A scandal at the center of the economy

If you don’t believe me, just read the news. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and CEO, was reinstated today by the company’s board after more than a week of whinging from shareholders, Silicon Valley leaders, and Trump. Huang had resigned in mid-November after allegations that he had had relationships with at least one employee, as well as a client who was allegedly an intelligence asset for the Chinese government. Trump, who was reportedly briefed multiple times about Huang’s affair with the suspected spy, intervened with the board to broker his return.

Because we live in an Nvidia-state, one man’s reinstatement was enough to change the trajectory of the entire stock market. Tech stocks, which sold off sharply late last week, rebounded aggressively. Nasdaq-100 futures went up so fast, they briefly halted trading this morning. Nvidia shares jumped 31 percent. The S&P 500 went up 4.7 percent, and the Nasdaq roared up 6.4 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,463 points. At the time of this writing, all three averages are on pace for their best day in 19 months.

The rationale for this rally is that Huang is the central figure of the AI boom—that Nvidia, which powers the AI economy and props it up with the company’s investments, is basically an exoskeleton around Huang. With him, AI progress and U.S. tech leadership can continue apace; without him, the music stops, investor confidence falters, and the AI bubble pops. On November 9, I wrote that, in the eyes of Silicon Valley and Trump, Huang was too big to fail. For 11 days—the window between Huang’s departure and his return—it looked like I was wrong and the shameless era of lol nothing matters in American politics and technology was winding down. Nope!

The professed logic of those calling for Huang’s return was nonsensical. The venture capitalists and shareholders argued that American dominance in the AI race against China depended on Huang’s ability to do whatever he pleased. This impunity included allowing Nvidia leeway to potentially skirt U.S. export controls and get chips into China, and sleeping with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. You might be forgiven for missing the genius of the argument.

Rather than control chip access to China, what the president and Silicon Valley’s most shameless leaders really seem to want is twofold. First, they—and especially Trump—want the circularly funded, debt-laden AI boom propping up the global economy to continue, in part because many of these AI companies have extremely large financial commitments on the books to keep purchasing chips. Second, they want to set a precedent. Huang’s return is a signal that those driving the AI boom are, in the eyes of the current administration and the market, above the law. To quote the president, “When you’re a star, they let you do it.”

Today, the elites got what they wished for. “The mistake has been corrected,” Elon Musk posted on X this morning. The investor Jason Calacanis, a co-host of the podcast All-In, posted, “Daddy’s home!” in reference to Trump stepping in to help the American economy. The hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman argued that “the wisdom of the crowd prevails,” which is an odd way to characterize the president of the United States intervening in a public company’s board meeting to agitate for a personnel change. It’s unclear exactly what Ackman means by “crowd” or even “wisdom.” On November 3, Americans expressed great skepticism at the polls about data centers, the economy, and AI in general. And a YouGov poll from earlier this month revealed that 54 percent of Americans thought that Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the alleged spy, “has definitely or probably compromised U.S. national security.” (Trump reportedly told Nvidia board members this week that this was not the case.)

But as we know now, the Nvidia-state is not a democracy. It doesn’t care that lawmakers in both parties—who will grill the CEO in December when he testifies in front of Congress—are livid about Huang’s reinstatement and publicly questioning Trump’s involvement. The Nvidia-state does not care about potential subpoenas or congressional investigations. It does not care what might come out about Huang, or Nvidia’s dealings with China, or chip smuggling. What the Nvidia-state cares about is the continued reliance of the economy on one industry, one company, and, seemingly, one man. In Nvidia-state, engine of progress drives you.

This is how it goes in an AI hostage economy. Progress, economic security, superintelligence, national security, you name it—all of it is dangled as a carrot for citizens. But all of it, including your retirement savings, is contingent, according to those in charge. Any bit of accountability or oversight could cause the whole thing to come crashing down. Progress squandered. Just keep calm and do what we say, and nobody gets hurt.

title: A Shameless Valley
summary: For 11 days this month, Silicon Valley gave the impression that it would finally, against all odds, subject itself to a genuine moment of shame. First, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having cheated on his wife with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy, putting his company, the AI in...
content:
For 11 days this month, Silicon Valley gave the impression that it would finally, against all odds, subject itself to a genuine moment of shame. First, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having cheated on his wife with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy, putting his company, the AI industry it undergirds, and the nation’s security at risk. He apologized profusely. Then it was reported that Huang had had another affair, this one with an Nvidia executive, and he resigned. It seemed that one of Silicon Valley’s titans was facing a reckoning.

But late last night, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social, “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang.” This outcome, the president wrote, “would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” Those words were evidently as much a command as they were a wish. This morning, Nvidia’s board of directors announced that it had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as CEO. The president then posted a meme that, even for him, was grotesque: a seemingly AI-generated image of Huang, face bloodied from a wound, raising a fist clenching a red brassiere with an Nvidia flag waving in the background—modeled, of course, on the photo taken just after the first assassination attempt on Trump. So much for shame.

[Read:A ]$5.7 Trillion Face-Plant

It’s worth underscoring just how damning Huang’s scandals were. He admitted to having a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman tied to a company that was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China—thereby sidestepping U.S. export controls—at the same time that he was lobbying tirelessly to ease restrictions meant to keep American chips out of the hands of Chinese competition. For a company in Nvidia’s position, it was an earth-shattering revelation: Nvidia essentially has a monopoly on the chips used to train the most advanced AI models. That has made the firm spectacularly wealthy—earlier this year, it was valued at a record $5.7 trillion. Huang, in turn, used that wealth to underwrite much of the AI economy, funding all manner of data centers and start-ups as a sort of financial backstop. Huang’s resignation was followed by one of the worst weeks on Wall Street in recent memory. Further reports since his resignation—of a third affair and an abusive management style—only made Huang come off worse. A similar scandal in almost any other industry would result in universal political condemnation and an attempt, by both the company and its peers, to distance themselves from the disgraced former executive.

But it’s just the opposite here. The New York Times has reported that Trump and Vice President Vance spent the weekend pushing Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang. Almost immediately after this morning’s announcement, Trump posted on Truth Social to celebrate “the correct and proper” decision to restore Huang, a “Great Patriot and National Treasure.”

The mood in Silicon Valley is ebullient: The company’s stock jumped by more than 30 percent on the news, and investors and tech executives have erupted in an ovation. “The wisdom of the crowd prevails,” the hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman wrote on X. Elon Musk, a vocal Huang supporter, added: “The mistake has been corrected.” Many of Silicon Valley’s most powerful characters seem vindicated—after all, they downplayed and dismissed Huang’s follies as simple mistakes and aberrations.

In fact, the whole thing—recklessness and scandal followed by impunity—is the norm in the tech world. Silicon Valley has developed a reputation for generosity and forgiveness when it comes to its own sins. Musk has appeared to endorse racist and xenophobic conspiracy theories but sits on a multitrillion-dollar empire of businesses. Meta has been credibly accused of fueling ethnic violence, enabling the spread of misinformation, and harming children through addictive product design—the latter for which it agreed to a major settlement this summer—but remains among the largest companies in the world, and is structured such that Mark Zuckerberg basically cannot be fired. Almost exactly three years ago, Sam Altman was fired from OpenAI for being “not consistently candid” with the firm’s board of directors, only to be reinstated within days after Microsoft and other major investors rallied behind him. Now the entire AI industry is rushing headlong to build products that are jeopardizing the internet as we know it and, per AI executives’ own warnings, could destroy the planet. Meanwhile, Anthropic employees, post–public offering, are estimated to be worth more than the bottom third of U.S. households.

Over the past week and a half, legions of tech CEOs came out in support of Huang. “America needs to have more Jensens,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas said last Monday. This morning, the investor Chamath Palihapitiya wrote on X that Nvidia’s decision “prevented a massive economic own goal.” Just business as usual for some of the wealthiest companies in the world. (Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) Altman, asked last week about whether he thought Huang should return, demurred but said he felt “personal strong empathy” for his (soon-to-be) fellow ex-ex-CEO. This morning, Altman posted a single word: “Jensen!”

Huang’s return underscores the most important and perhaps singular value driving Silicon Valley: winning. Today that means more chips and data centers, more powerful AI models, greater revenues, soaring stock prices and valuations. Integrity, candor, atonement, and consequences seem like secondary concerns. The repercussions of the industry’s failures—wild swings in the stock market, technologies that wreak havoc on other industries and individual lives, a corrosion of cultural decency—are for everyone else to manage. Personal victory also happens to be one of the president’s major motivations. Trump has aligned himself with every tech CEO he deems successful—Altman, Apple’s Tim Cook, and most of all Huang, who is once again arguably the most influential CEO in the world.

Earlier this year, in a now infamous interview, Huang said that “you’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser.” Today, Silicon Valley decided to embrace its once and future king, whatever mistakes he made. After just 11 days of losing, Huang woke up winning once again.

title: The President Is Acting Like He Works for China
summary: Updated at 6:06 p.m. ET on November 23, 2026Americans learned several things over the past few days. The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence, is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation t...
content:
Updated at 6:06 p.m. ET on November 23, 2026

Americans learned several things over the past few days. The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence, is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation that makes some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. Another is that China’s Communist regime has gotten its hands on the chips. The markets, as usual, have reconfirmed that they prefer profit to politics: Nvidia’s stock price jumped more than 30 percent on the news of Huang’s return.

But most important, Americans learned—yet again—that their president does not care about the national security of the United States. In fact, he is so aggressively resistant to any notion of security that his actions have become almost indistinguishable from those of a hostile foreign agent.

Step back for a moment and consider this sequence of events. The married Nvidia boss was caught in a sexual relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. (She is not related to Jensen, but I will use first names here to avoid confusion). Alice, during this affair, worked for Megaspeed, a company in Singapore. Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips, and then found ways to get them to China, despite U.S. export controls. She also reportedly maintained contacts with the Ministry of State Security, the Chinese intelligence agency, while carrying on with Jensen.

(Some reports call Alice an “agent” or a “spy,” others refer to her as an “asset.” The distinction makes little practical difference in Jensen’s case. Someone who is employed by an intelligence agency, has professional training, and may be acting under a false identity, is an officer. Agents and assets are people recruited from private life, outside of the organization, who have a cooperative relationship, in varying degrees, with such an agency but aren’t actually employed as spooks. Either way, Jensen was literally in bed with someone who was reportedly in bed with Chinese intelligence.)

[Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection]

All of this certainly looks bad. It gets worse. The United States government, including President Trump, was warned by American intelligence that Alice was entangled with Beijing. In fact, Trump was warned twice in seven months, including once during a briefing by Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May as Trump was headed to China for a state visit. This must have been awkward, because shortly afterward, Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One and joined the U.S. delegation for the trip to China.

Trump ignored these warnings—or more accurately, in classic Trump style, he pretended not to know about these issues. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he said, just before his most recent visit to China. “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

Clearly not. Nor did these warnings move Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, whose former company, Cantor Fitzgerald, has significant ties to Nvidia, including financing some of the firms that were buying its chips.

The company is now run by Lutnick’s son.

Trump’s reaction to all this? When Jensen was discovered and had to leave his company, Trump got right to work trying to put him back in the big chair at Nvidia. “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” Nvidia wasn’t having it: Internal sources at the company made clear to reporters that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated.

So what changed in a matter of days? Nothing, except that the president apparently brought the American intelligence community into the fray to give Jensen a clean bill of health. At least that’s how it sounds from the Nvidia board’s public statement: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

The national-security process is slow and deliberative for a reason; people with even modest clearances who have been accused of minor infractions have had to wait months, sometimes even going to court, before being allowed back to work. An executive working with some of America’s most exotic technology commits adultery with a foreign citizen who has ties to a hostile government, and is credibly accused of funneling highly restricted American technology to a hostile intelligence service—and the U.S. security mandarins give the guy a thumbs up after a week?

Trump likes Jensen, he likes money, he likes the markets, and he likes Lutnick and his family. So perhaps he told the American spooks to sound the all-clear so that Jensen could get back to work. Trump indicated as much today when he told CNBC that he spoke with Nvidia’s board members. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.”

In a statement on Truth Social, Trump said: “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” That means exactly nothing. Saying that Todd Blanche does not “possess evidence” is an artful formulation meaning that Blanche does not have a file in front of him from the intelligence community detailing Jensen’s acts, some of which might have been dangerous even if they were not “unlawful.” (As any government employee can tell you, any number of “lawful” activities, including carrying lots of debt or having emotional problems, can sink a clearance and a job.) And because of Trump’s pressure to clear Jensen, it’s unlikely he ever will.

Not only did Trump celebrate the Nvidia decision, but he noted that the board’s action possibly averted a worse outcome: Jensen Huang working for China. If Jensen was “mad” enough, Trump said during an interview today, he might have accepted an offer to lead a Chinese company, because the Nvidia boss has some of their “blood in him.” In other words, the United States just vouched for a man the president said might have defected to China if he hadn’t been given his job back.

[Jonathan Chait: Trump’s backing of Huang is not superintelligent]

To recap: After a top industrialist got caught in an affair with a woman who might have been using the affair to slip American technology to a U.S. enemy, the president declared that his own spies had cleared his pal, waved off the national-security damage, and left everyone, ostensibly, happy. And by “everyone,” I mean Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick, Nvidia stockholders, and Communist China.

Trump solved this problem in a way that would make a foreign spy or a lobbyist for a foreign government both impressed and envious. Enemy spooks, their agents, and their assets spend their lives trying to do what Trump did in a week. Jensen’s off the hook, and the stock has bounced back. (And the Chinese should give Alice a medal.)

This whole terrible situation shows in galling detail that Trump just doesn’t think very much about the interests of the United States. (It also suggests that he couldn’t care less about the recent election, in which corruption was a top issue for many voters). He makes no secret of his preference for his own relationships over America’s safety: When asked if Russian President Vladimir Putin was a “friend to America,” Trump shrugged and said, “I can’t speak to America.”

That’s because Trump, for all his flag-hugging nonsense, doesn’t think in terms of “America” or “China” or “Russia.” He is a globalist, in the very worst sense of the word: a man who cares nothing for states or peoples or ideologies, because he sees the world as just an interconnected group of companies and banks. Some of those companies are run by his friends, and those are the only peers who matter. Everyone else is just raw material or collateral damage; the masses are just ciphers who either obey him or obey someone else.

It is perhaps an insult to foreign agents to say that Trump is acting like them. Foreign agents work for countries, and care about them. They do what they do out of patriotism, however misguided they may be about the regimes they might serve. Trump has no such ideals. Trump’s business is Trump’s business, and everything else—including “national interest” and “national security”—are just meaningless phrases used by chumps and saps.

This article was updated to clarify the words agent, officer, and asset.

title: Why Trump Rescued Jensen Huang
summary: A presidency that operated by normal rules of ethics or even self-preservation would be scrambling to distance itself from the repercussions of the Nvidia scandal. Last night, The New York Times reported that a Chinese woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s once and future chief executi...
content:
A presidency that operated by normal rules of ethics or even self-preservation would be scrambling to distance itself from the repercussions of the Nvidia scandal. Last night, The New York Times reported that a Chinese woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s once and future chief executive, was in regular contact with China’s spy agency. The woman, Alice Huang, may have influenced the Nvidia CEO’s decision to sell advanced chips to companies that transferred them to China.

Donald Trump instead pushed to reinstate Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO, even going so far as to dial in to the company’s board meeting to push for Huang’s return, a demand the company was in no position to turn down.

Trump’s decision is overdetermined, as an academic might put it, by several Trumpian precepts. The president believes as a matter of principle that powerful men should not face repercussions for sexual misconduct. He also takes a relativistic view of corruption, seeing it as simply a normal way to do business. This mindset allows him to routinely smear any opponent as corrupt (everybody does it, right?) while simultaneously engaging in flagrant corruption himself (after all, everybody does it).

But perhaps the most significant Trumpian attribute at play is his disregard for the national interest. Nvidia was permitting its advanced chips to fall into Chinese hands. This may have violated American law, and the law serves a critical purpose: to prevent America’s most powerful global rival from gaining access to cutting-edge technology that might enable it to obtain economic and military dominance.

[Read: A $5.7 trillion face-plant]

Conservative Republicans, who tend to be the most hawkish politicians on China, are outraged by this, which may well turn out to have a decisive effect on the course of global leadership. The prospect of the U.S. losing the artificial-intelligence race to China out of an American businessman’s greed or libidinousness should leave them predictably furious.

Trump, however, does not seem to care whatsoever. Despite his occasional demagoguery against China, he seems to have little interest in competing against it. He proclaims his admiration of its dictator, Xi Jinping, more than any other world leader save Vladimir Putin, the Russian dictator. After a symbolic but fruitless meeting with the two partners last week, Trump giddily posted memes depicting the troika as global leaders akin to Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill.

Trump does not want China to exert global dominance, but he does not seem to view its ambitions with any concern. He told reporters last week that he talked about Huang with Xi: “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances and I’d love to be able to see him have—that’s a very important company to us. And he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies, and I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, Oh, brilliant, brilliant.”

In other words, Trump seems to be saying that he asked the president of China, the country that is suspected of running the honey-trap operation on Huang, whether Trump should bring back the CEO of Nvidia. Then, Trump would have us believe, the Chinese president agreed that reinstating the executive over which China is feared to have leverage would be a good idea. And Trump presented this agreement as an encouraging sign.

[Read: China’s intelligence coup in the AI war]

In a normal administration, the mere fact that the president is telling a private company whom to install as CEO would itself constitute an enormous scandal. In the current atmosphere, this is simply a background detail.

The most benign explanation for Huang’s restoration is that Trump cares more about keeping the stock market soaring than any American national-security interest. Less benign interpretations include the possibility that Trump’s inner circle has profited from Nvidia circumventing export controls.

Determining what in fact took place will likely consume months of reporting and Watergate-style oversight hearings from a Congress that, as of January, will no longer be controlled by the president’s lackeys. Going into damage-control mode would be rational.

Instead Trump apparently believes that he can train his supporters to align their instincts with his and define his behavior as good and correct, as he did with the Russia hoax, or the perfect phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, or the stolen 2020 election. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote on Truth Social this morning. He followed this up by sharing a depiction of the 2024 attempted assassination of himself in Butler, Pennsylvania, but with Huang in his place, bloodied and holding aloft a red bra. As long as the stock market goes up, Jensen Huang can sleep with all the Chinese spies he wants.

title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya

content:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

content:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
summary: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recordedMultiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and pi...
content:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

content:
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

content:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
